About.title: About
About.metaDescription: Dialectio is a map of how words sound in the world's languages and in Ukrainian dialects. How to read the map and where the data comes from.
About.intro: Dialectio shows on a map how the same concept is written, pronounced and sounds in the world's languages and in the dialects of Ukrainian. It is a popular-science project: it aims to spark curiosity, not to replace a dictionary.
About.numbers: On the map now: {concepts} concepts, {languages} languages, {dialects} dialects, {words} words and {recordings} recordings by real speakers.
About.how1: Type a word in any language and pick a suggestion: countries that have a translation light up and the words appear on the map.
About.how2: Zoom in on Ukraine or its neighbours: from a certain zoom level, words are shown per region instead of per country. Dialect words are purple.
About.how3: Click a country or region to keep only the languages and dialects spoken there in the panel.
About.how4: IPA in square brackets is the pronunciation in the International Phonetic Alphabet. The ▶ button plays a recording; TTS marks a synthetic voice.
About.how5: The ≈ mark means an unverified word: a draft, a Wikidata concept label or a machine translation. These may be inaccurate, and we are checking them step by step.
About.dialects: Dialects follow the classic scheme: three dialect groups (Northern, South-Western, South-Eastern) and 15 dialects. Dialect areas are approximated by regions, which is a simplification: real dialect borders do not follow administrative ones. Lemko and Nadsian are also shown in Poland and Slovakia.
About.help: Do you know how this word is said in your village or town? Click “Know how it’s said where you live?” in the word panel, type the word and, if you like, record it. Contributions appear on the site after an editor reviews them.
About.feedback: Spotted a mistake? Tell us on <link>GitHub</link>.

Sources.title: Sources and licenses
Sources.metaDescription: Where Dialectio gets its words, pronunciations, audio and maps, and under which licenses.
Sources.intro: Every word and recording on the site keeps its source. The license and author of each recording are shown in the tooltip of its ▶ button.
Sources.name: Source
Sources.map: Country and region borders come from Natural Earth (public domain), in the Ukrainian point-of-view edition. Basemap: OpenFreeMap, © OpenMapTiles, data © OpenStreetMap contributors (ODbL). The map is rendered with MapLibre GL.
Sources.tts: Where no real recording exists, pronunciation is synthesized with Piper, using only voices whose license allows this use. These recordings are marked TTS.
Sources.own: Words added by editors, drafts and Dialectio's machine translations are protected by copyright (all rights reserved). Visitor contributions are published with their permission.

Privacy.title: Privacy policy
Privacy.metaDescription: What data Dialectio collects and how it is used.
Privacy.intro: You can use Dialectio without an account. We show no ads and use no trackers.
Privacy.contrib: We store what you enter in the form: the word, the language or dialect, the place, your name (optional) and a voice recording (optional). Your name and place may be shown next to the word after review. By sending a contribution you allow Dialectio to publish it.
Privacy.ip: To fight spam, the server temporarily remembers how many contributions came from an IP address in the last hour. This is not written to the database.
Privacy.browser: The site remembers in your browser (localStorage) the dialect you last picked in the contribution form, so you don't have to pick it again. This is not sent to us.
Privacy.third: The basemap is loaded from OpenFreeMap servers and some audio from Wikimedia Commons. These services see your IP address, like any site your browser loads something from.
Privacy.delete: To delete your contribution or voice recording, write to us on <link>GitHub</link> with the word and the dialect.

Dialects.title: Dialects of Ukrainian
Dialects.metaDescription: Three dialect groups and 15 dialects of Ukrainian: where they are spoken and which words they use, with a map, translations and pronunciation.
Dialects.intro: Ukrainian dialects fall into three groups. Pick a dialect to see its area on the map and its words with standard Ukrainian equivalents.
Dialects.pageDescription: {name}: {examples} and more words with standard Ukrainian equivalents. Its area on the map, pronunciation.
Dialects.territoryNote: Areas are approximated by regions; real dialect borders do not follow administrative ones.
Dialects.noWords: No words for this dialect yet. Open any word and click “Know how it’s said where you live?”.
Dialects.unverifiedNote: ≈ — unverified word: a draft not yet checked by an editor.

DialectInfo.ukr-polissia-west: The West Polissian dialect is spoken in the Polissia of Volyn and Rivne. It has diphthongs and other vowels in place of old o and e (кунь, нуч for кінь, ніч) and old vocabulary shared with Belarusian dialects.
DialectInfo.ukr-polissia-central: The Central Polissian dialect is spoken in northern Zhytomyr and Kyiv regions. Stressed old o and e turn into diphthongs: куонь, нуоч.
DialectInfo.ukr-polissia-east: The East Polissian dialect is spoken in the Chernihiv region and northern Sumy. It has diphthongs like куінь and much in common with neighbouring Russian and Belarusian dialects.
DialectInfo.ukr-volhynian: The Volhynian dialect is spoken in southern Volyn and Rivne and western Zhytomyr. It is transitional between the Polissian and Podillian dialects.
DialectInfo.ukr-podillian: The Podillian dialect is spoken in the Vinnytsia and Khmelnytskyi regions. Known for words like пшінка (maize) and бараболя (potato).
DialectInfo.ukr-dniester: The Dniester dialect is spoken along the Dniester in the Lviv, Ternopil and Ivano-Frankivsk regions. Many loans from Polish and German: ровер (bicycle), шклянка (glass), склеп (shop).
DialectInfo.ukr-nadsian: The Nadsian dialect is spoken along the San river: western Lviv region and Subcarpathia in Poland. It is close to the Dniester and Lemko dialects.
DialectInfo.ukr-boyko: The Boyko dialect is spoken in the mountains of the Lviv and Ivano-Frankivsk regions. Typical words: хижа (house), облак (window), ногавиці (trousers).
DialectInfo.ukr-hutsul: The Hutsul dialect is spoken in the Carpathians: Ivano-Frankivsk, Bukovyna, Transcarpathia and Maramureș in Romania. Known for words like ґазда (master), ватра (fire), полонина (mountain meadow).
DialectInfo.ukr-pokuttia-bukovyna: The Pokuttia-Bukovyna dialect is spoken in Bukovyna (Chernivtsi region and Suceava in Romania) and Pokuttia. Many Romanian loans: патлажан (tomato), папушой (maize).
DialectInfo.ukr-transcarpathian: The Transcarpathian dialect is spoken in Transcarpathia. Many Hungarian and Slovak loans: крумплі (potato), уборка (cucumber), погар (glass).
DialectInfo.ukr-lemko: The Lemko dialect is spoken in Lemkivshchyna: the Polish Carpathians (Lesser Poland, Subcarpathia) and the Prešov region of Slovakia. Written with the letter ы: хыжа, лыжка.
DialectInfo.ukr-middle-dnieper: The Middle Dnieper dialect is spoken in the Kyiv, Cherkasy and Poltava regions. It is the basis of modern standard Ukrainian, so it differs from it the least.
DialectInfo.ukr-slobozhan: The Slobozhan dialect is spoken in the Kharkiv and Sumy regions. Close to the Middle Dnieper dialect, with noticeable Russian influence.
DialectInfo.ukr-steppe: The Steppe dialect is spoken in southern and eastern Ukraine: Zaporizhzhia, Kherson, Mykolaiv, Odesa, Donetsk. The youngest dialect, formed by settlers from many regions.
